items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 23, 2026
items.excerpt: Democrats have secured 258 seats in the US House of Representatives following the Nov. 3 midterm elections, marking their strongest performance in the chamber in over three decades, according to election results reported by the Associated Press. The party reached the milestone after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th Congressional District following a recount. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes out of approximately 287,000 cast, according to AP. The victory brought Democrats' total gains to 44 seats nationwide, surpassing the 40 seats the party gained in the 2018 midterm elections during President Donald Trump's first term.

The protests were led by workers and students and were part of a wave of actions across Europe over the weekend. > Laura Peritore: “Young people and students across Europe are mobilizing today for this strike against rearmament, against military conscription and against the cuts being made to healthcare and public spending, while billions are being invested in weapons.” Tens of thousands marched in Paris over the cost of living, disinvestment in public services and political gridlock ahead of next year’s presidential election. Virginia Foxx In North Carolina, Democrat Chuck Hubbard has narrowly defeated 11-term Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx. Hubbard’s win gives Democrats at least 259 seats in the next Congress — its largest total since after the 1992 elections. Three U.S. House races remain uncalled. ## Army Plans “Controlled Detonation” of Toxic Material at Iowa Ammunition Plant, Despite Court Order The U.S. Army is planning to blow up nearly five tons of a toxic lead-containing compound at an ammunition plant in Iowa — despite a court order that put the initial detonation on hold. The Army had been planning to carry out what it called a “controlled” detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, today. items.title: Fed Watches Inflation Picture Turn Uglier | Charles Schwab
items.excerpt: November 23, 2026• Henry Hoenig In late October, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said policymakers wanted more information before agreeing to raise interest rates again. At least some of what they've seen hasn't been pretty. Yes, the rise in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) decelerated from 0.6% month over month in September to 0.4% in October. But energy accounted for 58% of September's rise, while in October it accounted for only 15%, making energy a relatively minor factor in the latest reading. Still, October's gain works out to annualized inflation of about 4.3%. Zooming out also reveals a less-than-attractive picture. Over the three months through October, CPI rose an annualized 5.7%, while the wholesale Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand rose an annualized 9%. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose at a 3.7% annualized rate during the same period. That's more than double the 1.6% pace it set in the three months through July. Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price data for October is due November 25. PCE is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. But Fed Governor Christopher J. Waller didn't wait for it. Hours before the CPI release on November 10, he said that if October CPI rose 0.3% or more, the Fed should consider raising rates by a half percentage point at its December meeting to maintain its inflation-fighting credibility. Waller, who voted to hold rates steady in October, noted particular concern about the breadth of price increases. ## Inflation spreads? Inflation appears to be spreading. In October, 105 of 177 CPI expenditure categories (59%) rose faster than a 3% annualized rate. That equals the highest level since August 2022, up from 49% in September and 46% in August. In all, 27 categories rose the most in at least a year, including household furnishings and supplies (up 0.7% month over month), motor vehicle insurance (up 0.7%), and club memberships and sports fees (up 1.2%). Several regional Fed gauges that track the underlying inflation trend have turned up again, reaching the highest levels since May. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's core sticky-price index, which excludes food and energy and tracks slower-moving items, rose at a one-month annualized rate of 4.7% in October. ... Oil and gasoline prices have fallen somewhat, and that'll help. But global refinery constraints have caused diesel prices to diverge somewhat from oil prices, and diesel feeds into inflation via more channels than gasoline does. Diesel powers the trucks that deliver goods and the farm machinery used to grow food. As of November 16, diesel prices were down only 9% from their record high set in September, compared to a 22% decline for WTI crude oil from its October high. October's PPI data showed that truck freight rates rose 3.9% from a month earlier and 25% from a year earlier, while wholesale food prices rose 1.3% from a month earlier, the fastest increase since February.

items.title: US business activity growth eases further in November, survey shows By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 23 (Reuters) - US business activity growth slowed further in November as high prices held back new orders and capacity constraints restrained output, but overall activity remains resilient, suggesting economic growth is continuing at an above-trend rate, a survey showed on Monday. S&P Global said its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, tracking the manufacturing and services sectors, eased to a four-month low of 54.6 this month from a final reading of 55.9 in October. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. The pace of growth slackened in both manufacturing and the vast services sector, which is responsible for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity. The manufacturing PMI slipped to a three-month low of 54.5 from 54.9 in October, while the services PMI dropped to a four-month low of 54.7 from 56.1 last month. New business in services slid, while new orders in manufacturing were little changed. Input cost pressures eased but remain elevated and suggest inflation overall will stay well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. "Although output growth slowed in November, recent readings have been impressively strong, and the PMI surveys still point to GDP (gross domestic product) rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Growth also remained encouragingly broad-based across both manufacturing and services, with both sectors also still taking on additional staff in numbers that are indicative of a further strong payroll gain during November." The US economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter thanks to ongoing strength in consumer spending and the frenetic artificial intelligence build-out, and employers added a greater-than-expected 165,000 workers to their payrolls in October. "A key concern is the elevated cost of living and resulting pressures on affordability, and the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed’s 2% target in the coming months, despite some moderation of the rate of inflation in November," Williamson said. "Supply disruptions, widely linked to global shipping delays, also appear to have become more widespread, adding to firms’ concerns about being able to fulfill orders and likely to add further to underlying price pressures in the coming months." The November 12-20 survey period also dovetailed with a sharp selloff in the US stock market, which has been a key pillar supporting consumer spending, on concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. It was not clear from the survey data whether that development contributed to the softening in this month’s PMI readings.
